raw_response:
I farm only 3 mu, so I do not chase the highest possible yield. I need the land to stay reliable and the cash use to stay manageable. I have done wheat-maize for many years, and with well water available, I would keep that system this year. Because my education is relatively high and I have seen enough seasons, I adjust a little by crop stage, but I still stay close to what has worked on my own fields. For wheat, I want a steady stand before winter, enough base fertilizer to support tillering, then one topdress at jointing if the seedlings look strong enough to carry yield. I will irrigate at the key stages, but not excessively, because pumping costs money and too much water can make lodging worse. For maize, the turnaround after wheat is very tight, so I will not do heavy tillage. I will clear the wheat quickly, do shallow rotary tillage or direct sow if the machine is available, and use a hybrid seed that emerges fast. I prefer to keep fertilizer split, with most nitrogen going on around the jointing stage for wheat and around the big flare stage for maize, because that gives me better use of fertilizer than one heavy dose up front. With some family members working off-farm, I will rely mainly on family labor for supervision and small jobs, and use machinery or short hired help only in the tight wheat-maize transition if needed.
